n: Benjamin receives a fuller genealogy, because it was the tribe of King Saul and, with Judah, formed the core of the southern kingdom and the community after the exile.
Benjamin’s five sons, listed in birth order. The names differ in places from the lists in Genesis and Numbers, perhaps reflecting clans at different times.

f.g: A Benjamite clan head; not related to the Rephaim giants.

n: Bela’s sons include Gera, an ancestor name shared by the judge Ehud and by Shimei, who cursed David.
More of Bela’s descendants, among them a Naaman—not the Syrian general healed by Elisha.
The list of Bela’s sons concludes.

f.g: Also called Shupham or Shuppim (Numbers 26:39).

n: Ehud’s clans lived at Geba but were later relocated to Manahath. The text hints at a migration or conflict it does not explain.

f.g: Moved them, perhaps forcibly, to another place.

n: Gera led this move, and his line continued through Uzza and Ahihud.

f.g: Probably Gera, who led the relocation.

n: Shaharaim had children in Moab after divorcing two wives. Ruth’s story shows other contact between Israel and Moab in early times.

f.g: Divorced them.

n: Shaharaim’s sons by his wife Hodesh in Moab. Some names, like Mesha, match known Moabite names.

f.g: Also the name of a famous Moabite king (2 Kings 3:4), though not the same man.

n: These sons became family leaders.

f.g: Heads of clans or ancestral houses.

n: Shaharaim also had sons by his earlier wife Hushim.

f.g: “God has worked”; his family is traced in the next verses.

n: Elpaal’s son Shamed built Ono and Lod, towns in the coastal lowlands. Lod became Lydda in the New Testament, where Peter healed Aeneas.
Beriah and Shema led the people of Aijalon and drove out Gath’s inhabitants—perhaps an echo of conflict reported in chapter 7.

f.w: drove away the inhabitants of Gath

n: More Benjamite families begin to be listed by their founders.

f.g: His sons are listed in verses 22–25.

n: The list continues; Arad is also the name of a town in the Negev.

f.g: A personal name here; also a Canaanite city in the south (Numbers 21:1).

n: These are the sons of Beriah.

f.g: Beriah of Aijalon, from verse 13.

n: The sons of Elpaal begin to be listed.

f.g: A short form of Hezekiah, “the LORD strengthens.”

n: These are Elpaal’s sons, Benjamite family heads.

f.g: Elpaal of verses 11–12.

n: The sons of Shimhi begin.

f.g: “Remembered”; a name that appears several times in this chapter.

n: More of Shimhi’s sons, two of whose names honor God (Eli-).

f.g: “My God is God.”

n: These are the sons of Shimhi, probably the same as Shema of verse 13.

f.g: Possibly Shema of verse 13.

n: The sons of Shashak begin.

f.g: A common name meaning “companion” or “associate.”

n: More sons of Shashak.

f.g: “Gracious.”

n: Antothijah’s name may link him to the town of Anathoth.

f.g: Perhaps “the Anathothite,” from the town of Anathoth.

n: These were the sons of Shashak, Benjamite clan leaders.

f.g: “Face of God”; also the place where Jacob wrestled (Genesis 32:30).

n: The sons of Jeroham begin, including a man named Athaliah—a name more famous for a wicked queen.

f.g: Here a man’s name; the name was used for both men and women.

n: Jeroham’s sons complete this list of Benjamite families.
These clan heads lived in Jerusalem, which lay on the border of Benjamin and Judah.
The chronicler turns to Gibeon, a town northwest of Jerusalem, where Saul’s ancestors lived. The Gibeonites had tricked Joshua into a peace treaty long before.

f.g: The founder or leading clan head of Gibeon, named Jeiel in 1 Chronicles 9:35.

n: His sons include Kish, a family name in Saul’s line.

f.g: A Kish, uncle of Saul’s father Kish; family names often repeated.

n: More sons of Gibeon’s founder.

f.g: Called Zechariah in 1 Chronicles 9:37.

n: Mikloth’s family lived near their relatives in Jerusalem.

f.g: Near or alongside them.

n: Here is Saul’s family tree: from Ner and Kish to Saul and his sons. Esh-baal is better known as Ish-bosheth, who briefly ruled after Saul.

f.g: “Man of Baal,” meaning “man of the Lord”; later writers changed it to Ish-bosheth, “man of shame.”

n: Jonathan’s son Merib-baal is Mephibosheth, the lame prince whom David treated with kindness for Jonathan’s sake.

f.g: Called Mephibosheth in 2 Samuel, again replacing “baal” with “bosheth” (shame).
Called Mica in 2 Samuel 9:12.

n: Saul’s line continued through Micah’s four sons.
The line of Saul continues for several more generations, showing that his house survived.

f.g: Also the name of a Benjamite town near Jerusalem (Ezra 2:24).

n: The descendants continue through Moza, Binea and others.

f.g: His six sons are named in the next verse.

n: Azel’s six sons are listed—about twelve generations after Saul.
The family of Azel’s brother Eshek is listed too.

f.g: Mentioned only here.

n: Ulam’s sons were brave archers with many descendants. Benjamin was known for skilled marksmen; centuries later the apostle Paul proudly called himself a Benjamite.

f.w: All these are of the sons of Benjamin
